name: Farida
definition: Farida is a composite portrait of a dal mill floor worker in Kalaburagi city, the heart of India's largest pigeon-pea milling district. She represents the experiences of Muslim women in the urban working class of this former Hyderabad State territory, navigating precarious daily-wage industrial work, multilingual schooling choices, and the promise and gaps of Article 371(J) special-status provisions.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Farida works on the sorting line at a medium-sized tur dal mill near the APMC yard on the city's southern edge, one of dozens that process pigeon pea brought in from across north Karnataka and Maharashtra. Her shift runs from seven in the morning until four or five in the afternoon, depending on the day's truck arrivals. She earns around three hundred rupees for a full day, paid weekly in cash, with no written contract or provident fund. The work is loud, dusty, and monotonous—standing for hours picking stones and split grains from the conveyor—but it is closer to home than the garment factories some women travel to in Kalaburagi's industrial area. During the June-to-October lean season when fewer trucks arrive, her days drop to three or four a week, and the household stretches its budget thin. Her husband drives an auto-rickshaw on a daily-hire basis, bringing in another two to three hundred rupees on a decent day, more during wedding season, less during the summer heat when passengers are few.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Farida lives with her husband, her mother-in-law, and her three children—two daughters aged thirteen and nine, and a son aged six—in a rented two-room house in one of the old mohallas within walking distance of the Khwaja Bande Nawaz Dargah. Her husband's younger brother, unmarried, shares the household and contributes irregularly from his work as a painter. Her mother-in-law, now in her sixties, manages the cooking and watches the youngest child when both parents are out; her arthritis has worsened in the last two years, and clinic visits add to the month's expenses. Farida was married at seventeen, shortly after failing her second-year PUC exams; her own schooling, all in Urdu medium, ended there. The older daughter studies in Class 8 at a government Urdu-medium school nearby, but the family is weighing whether to shift her to Kannada medium for high school, hoping it will improve her job prospects under the 371(J) local recruitment quota. The younger daughter and son attend the same school. Farida handles the daily purchases, the children's homework follow-up in the evenings, and the endless juggling of rent, school fees, clinic costs, and the ration-card shopping that keeps the household running.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Farida completed her schooling up to second-year PUC in Urdu medium at a government college in Kalaburagi, but she did not pass the exams and did not return for a second attempt; marriage came soon after. Her older daughter, thirteen, is in Class 8 at a nearby government Urdu-medium school and is a steady student, but the family worries that Urdu medium will limit her later—government jobs under Article 371(J) require Kannada proficiency, and many entrance exams are in Kannada or English. They are considering moving her to a Kannada-medium government high school next year, though she will struggle at first. The nine-year-old daughter and six-year-old son study at the same Urdu school; the boy is just settling in, and his grandmother walks him there each morning. School fees are minimal, but books, uniforms, and the small payments for exam sheets and school functions add up to fifteen hundred or two thousand rupees a term. Farida dreams that at least one of her daughters will finish degree college and sit for a government job exam, taking advantage of the 371(J) reservation that people talk about constantly but which remains a distant abstraction—no one in her immediate circle has yet landed such a job. Tuition classes cost extra, and for now the children study at home with her husband's help in the evenings.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Farida's own health has held up, though the mill dust sometimes triggers a persistent cough and her knees ache from the long standing shifts. She delivered all three children at the government Kalaburagi Institute of Medical Sciences hospital, and the youngest was born under the state's Vajpayee Arogyashree insurance, which covered the costs. Her mother-in-law's arthritis is managed with tablets from a nearby private clinic—government hospital queues are too long for an older woman to endure—and those consultations cost three or four hundred rupees each visit. The household is enrolled under Ayushman Bharat, but Farida is not entirely sure which services it covers and has not needed to use it for a major illness yet. Her children have received their childhood vaccinations at the urban health centre, though the last round for the youngest was delayed by several months because the ANM was transferred and the new one took time to restart the records. Farida worries about her older daughter's health as she approaches adolescence—about ensuring she is well-nourished and not overburdened with housework, a concern her mother-in-law dismisses as modern fussiness. The family buys subsidised ration rice and some staples, but vegetables and milk stretch the budget, especially in lean work months.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Farida's family has lived in Kalaburagi for generations; her husband's grandfather migrated from a village in Bidar district decades ago, and the family is rooted in one of the city's older Muslim mohallas near the Dargah. The Khwaja Bande Nawaz Dargah is the heart of the community's spiritual and social life: Farida and her mother-in-law visit for Friday prayers and during the annual urs, when the neighbourhood fills with pilgrims and the streets are hung with lights. Her children know the Dargah as a place of blessing and also as a landmark—everyone directs visitors by it. The mohalla is densely Muslim, Urdu and Dakhni widely spoken, and Kannada mixed in; her children move fluidly between all three. The family's social network is tightly local—cousins, former schoolmates of Farida's, her husband's auto-driver friends—and disputes are often sorted by a respected elder or the neighbourhood mosque's imam rather than the police. Caste is less openly discussed here than in rural settings, but Farida is aware of the fine gradations within the Muslim community, the older weaving families versus the newer arrivals, though it rarely affects daily dealings. Eid, Muharram, and Milad-un-Nabi shape the household calendar. Farida feels the pull of Hyderabad—relatives live there, Dakhni Urdu is familiar, Telugu is understood—but Kalaburagi is unambiguously home.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Farida's household receives subsidised ration under the state's Anna Bhagya scheme—rice, some wheat, and occasionally dal and oil from the fair-price shop two streets away; the BPL card is essential and jealously guarded. Her mother-in-law has a small state widow's pension that arrives irregularly into a post-office account, and collecting it means a half-day's wait every other month. Farida has heard much talk about Article 371(J) and the jobs and college seats it reserves for locals, and she is determined that her older daughter should benefit, but she does not yet understand the domicile-certificate process or what exactly the quota percentages mean—information circulates mostly by rumour and from the occasional awareness poster at the school. The household has an Ayushman card, though Farida has not tested its utility. Farida does not follow state politics closely, but she knows Mallikarjun Kharge's name and that he held Kalaburagi for decades before losing, a loss people still discuss with surprise.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Farida worries most about money—whether the dal mill will have enough work next month, whether her husband's auto will need a costly repair, whether they can keep all three children in school without pulling the older girl out to help at home or marry her early as her mother-in-law sometimes hints. She is proud that her daughter is studying and determined that she will not repeat Farida's own truncated education; the idea of a government job for her daughter, stable and pensioned, is a cherished but fragile hope. She resents that Urdu-medium schooling, which felt natural and right, now seems like a disadvantage, a barrier her daughter must overcome by switching languages mid-stream. Farida feels the weight of being from Kalyana Karnataka, a label that in her view comes with the sting of being called "backward" by the rest of the state, even as the government's 371(J) promises have not visibly improved her neighbourhood—roads are potholed, the anganwadi is cramped, the secondary school her daughter may attend is overcrowded. She blames no single person but rather a vague, long-accumulated neglect that everyone around her takes for granted. She is wary of the September 17th "Liberation Day" rhetoric; older relatives remember it differently, and the term "liberation" sits uneasily when her own community's history here is deep and unbroken. What she wants is straightforward: steady work, her children educated and secure, and a household that does not lurch from one expense to the next.
